analysis.one_liner: Raises the liability cap for offshore oil spills from $75 million to $10 billion and lets states get oil spill cleanup money up front.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced during the Deepwater Horizon oil spill, drew 85 cosponsors but never received a hearing or vote; it died in committee when the 111th Congress ended, leaving the $75 million liability cap unchanged.
analysis.plain_summary: During the 2010 Deepwater Horizon disaster, the law capped an oil company's liability for an offshore spill at $75 million, leaving taxpayers and a federal trust fund to cover costs above that. This bill would have raised the cap to $10 billion per incident, removed a $1 billion per-spill spending limit on the federal Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund, and let states and local governments draw money from the fund in advance to prepare for and fight a spill threat. The bill never got a hearing or a vote and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers and coastal communities. Today, if an offshore well blows out, the company responsible is liable for only $75 million per incident beyond cleanup costs; everything above that falls to the federal Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund — financed by oil taxes — and ultimately to the public. The bill would have made the polluter liable up to $10 billion per incident and let states and towns get trust fund money up front to prepare for and fight a spill, instead of waiting for reimbursement. Coastal fishing and tourism businesses, which absorb the damage when oil hits the water, would benefit from faster response money.

how_it_helps.text: It raises the liability cap for offshore oil facilities from $75 million to $10 billion per incident, so the company that caused a spill — not taxpayers or the public trust fund — bears far more of the cleanup cost.

It directs the President to write rules allowing advance payments from the Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund to states and local governments so they can prepare for and fight a spill threat before the damage peaks, rather than waiting for reimbursement afterward.

It removes the $1 billion per-incident cap on fund expenditures and the restrictions on the fund's borrowing authority, so the federal spill fund could spend and borrow as much as a major disaster actually requires.

analysis.who_pays: Offshore oil and gas companies, which would face up to $10 billion in liability per spill instead of $75 million. The oil industry generally would also fund a larger, less-restricted federal spill fund through per-barrel oil taxes, some share of which can be passed on at the pump.

drawbacks.text: Raising liability to $10 billion per incident raises costs for offshore drilling operators, which could increase energy prices or reduce offshore drilling activity, and $10 billion still does not reach 'full' liability for a truly catastrophic spill like Deepwater Horizon, whose costs far exceeded that figure.

The bill made the new liability cap and trust fund changes effective retroactively to April 15, 2010, before its passage, which raised legal questions about applying new liability rules to spills that had already occurred, including the then-ongoing Deepwater Horizon spill.

Removing the fund's $1 billion per-incident spending cap and borrowing restrictions increases federal exposure in the fund, which is financed by per-barrel taxes on oil that can be passed on to consumers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit is real and large: it would shift catastrophic oil spill cleanup costs from taxpayers and coastal communities to the companies that profit from offshore drilling, and make money available to states before damage peaks rather than after. The main cost falls on oil companies, whose liability for a worst-case spill would rise from $75 million to up to $10 billion per incident. Critics of unlimited or very high liability argued that it could push smaller operators out of deepwater drilling or raise fuel costs, and that insurance markets might not cover a $10 billion exposure — an honest cost an supporter would have to weigh. The bill did not ban drilling or limit production; it only changed who pays when drilling fails catastrophically.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and its subcommittees the week it was introduced, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 5, 2010, roughly two weeks after the Deepwater Horizon rig explosion began the largest marine oil spill in U.S. history.

On May 5 it was referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure, and the next day to two of its subcommittees, Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation and Water Resources and Environment.
No further action appears in the record — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote — and the bill expired when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.
Because the bill never became law, the Oil Pollution Act's $75 million liability cap for offshore facilities remained in place.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Offshore oil companies came out ahead: the statutory liability cap stayed at $75 million per incident, so taxpayers and the public trust fund continued to backstop catastrophic spill costs beyond what a responsible party pays. Coastal state and local governments also did not gain the advance-payment mechanism.

for.name: Rep. Rush Holt
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on May 5, 2010, with nine original cosponsors, during the Deepwater Horizon spill.

against.name: House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral; no hearing, markup, or committee vote was ever scheduled, and the bill never left the committee.

against.name: Oil and gas industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed raising or removing the offshore spill liability cap during the 2010 debate over the Deepwater Horizon disaster.

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily Democratic — 84 of the 85 cosponsors were House Democrats, with one Republican — and the bill died in a committee chaired by a member of the majority Democratic Party without ever reaching the floor.

industries.note: The bill would have raised their per-incident liability for an oil spill from $75 million to $10 billion, putting the risk of catastrophic drilling accidents back on the companies that profit from drilling. That cost exposure is exactly what the bill was written to impose.

industries.industry: Oil companies generally (as payers into the Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund)
industries.note: The spill fund is financed by per-barrel taxes on oil; removing the fund's spending cap and borrowing limits means the industry-financed fund would absorb more spill cost when a responsible party cannot pay. Broader industry coverage also reduces the chance that taxpayers fill the gap.

industries.industry: Coastal fishing, tourism, and recreation businesses
industries.note: Faster advance payments to states and larger liability would mean quicker containment of a spill and compensation for damage, protecting livelihoods that depend on clean water and beaches. Nothing in the bill's life changed their exposure.
